title: Q Anon: When Wild Conspiracy Went (sort of) Mainstream
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the QAnon conspiracy movement: its core claims about a Satanic, pedophile, cannibal global elite opposing Donald Trump, its roots in older antisemitic conspiracy theories like the blood libel and the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, and its origins in Pizzagate (2016) and the anonymous Q drops on 4chan and 8chan starting October 2017. They cover the Comet Ping Pong shooting, the cryptic "breadcrumb" drops and "baking" interpretation, the spread to mainstream social media and the pandemic-era surge, Trump's ambiguous engagement with QAnon, the identity of Q (Paul Ferber, then Ron and James Watkins, with Frederick Brennan as critic), real-world violence linked to the movement, its persistence after the 2020 election and the 2024 assassination attempt, and advice for families of believers. The episode closes with listener mail about a glasses episode.

entities.name: Protocols of the Elders of Zion

segments.title: Opening and ground rules
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, which had sat in their folder for years, and set the approach of treating QAnon beliefs as untrue while explaining them anthropologically.

segments.title: Defining QAnon and its antisemitic roots
segments.summary: QAnon is described as an online conspiracy theory about a global elite cabal. Its roots are traced to the blood libel and the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, and the cabal is said to include celebrities and politicians.
topics: Protocols of the Elders of Zion

segments.title: Core beliefs: the cabal and Trump as savior
segments.summary: The hosts list the alleged cabal members, including the Clintons, Tom Hanks, Oprah Winfrey, George Soros and others, and describe the belief that Donald Trump was secretly chosen to fight them and that a coming storm will bring martial law and a Great Awakening.

segments.title: Lizard people, adrenochrome and breadcrumbs
segments.summary: Additional beliefs include lizard people and adrenochrome as an elixir of life, which the hosts say is a misreading of Hunter Thompson's book. The hosts then explain Q's breadcrumbs and the practice of baking them into consensus theories.
topics: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas

segments.title: Pizzagate and the Comet Ping Pong shooting
segments.summary: Pizzagate began in 2016 when a Podesta email mentioning a pizza restaurant was circulated on 4chan as evidence of a child trafficking hub. A man drove from North Carolina and fired an AR-15 inside Comet Ping Pong in December 2016, and was later jailed.

segments.title: Origins of the Q drops on 4chan
segments.summary: The first Q drop was posted October 2017 on 4chan under the name Q Clearance Patriot. Drops were cryptic, used initials and referred to Barack Obama as Hussein, and centered on the Hillary Clinton email scandal and the Loretta Lynch tarmac meeting.

segments.title: Spread to mainstream social media and the pandemic surge
segments.summary: The movement moved from 8chan to mainstream social media and news coverage, with documentaries and books legitimizing it. Activity spiked in March 2020 during the pandemic, when lockdown-era time and social media spread the theories.

segments.title: Save the Children hashtag and Wayfair rumor
segments.summary: Hashtags like Save the Children were hijacked from anti-trafficking efforts to pull people in. The Wayfair cabinet-price rumor showed how coincidences were turned into evidence of child trafficking.

segments.title: Trump's ambiguous engagement and the breadcrumb reading
segments.summary: Trump was asked about QAnon in August 2020 and did not reject it; his pink ties, Fiji water drinking and reposts of QAnon content since 2022 were read as signals. Trump distanced himself at rallies in 2019 before embracing the movement, and the hosts discuss how unfalsifiable beliefs resist correction.

segments.title: Break before the identity of Q
Who is Q: Paul Ferber and the Watkins family
segments.summary: Q is thought to have been South African Paul Ferber first, then control passed to James and Ron Watkins, who owned and ran 8chan. Frederick Brennan, 8chan's original creator, became a critic and source on Q's identity.

segments.title: The open-source cult and real-world violence
segments.summary: After Q stopped posting, the movement grew without Q. Violent acts linked to QAnon are described, including an armored truck blockade at the Hoover Dam, the 2021 killing of Gambino boss Francesco Cali, and others.

segments.title: Motives of Q's creators and further violence
segments.summary: The hosts wonder whether Q's authors believed the claims or were hoaxers. They describe a 2021 California killing of two children tied to reptilian beliefs and the attack on Paul Pelosi.

segments.title: Post-election persistence, 2024 assassination attempt and polling
segments.summary: After Trump lost in 2020, believers rationalized the outcome, and the 2024 assassination attempt in Pennsylvania was read as divine protection. Michael Flynn reportedly called QAnon a CIA psyop. Polls show QAnon beliefs held by 15 percent in May 2021 and rising by eight points by 2023.

segments.title: Helping friends and family who fell into QAnon
segments.summary: Hosts describe how families who stayed nonjudgmental helped believers return, and mention the Anti-Defamation League as a resource.

segments.title: Listener mail: four eyes bad
segments.summary: Listener Marty explains that the phrase four eyes bad in the earlier glasses episode is a nod to George Orwell's Animal Farm, with the hosts praising the reference.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address and close the show.
